variables.meaning: the strength of the magnetic field the charge moves through, defined by the force it exerts on that charge
the magnetic force on the moving charge, perpendicular to the plane formed by the velocity and the field
the charge that moves through the field; the force reverses when the sign of the charge reverses
the speed of the charge through the field; a charge at rest feels no magnetic force
the angle between the direction of the velocity and the direction of the magnetic field
the radius of the circle a charge follows when it moves perpendicular to a uniform field
the mass of the charged particle, which sets how wide its circle is at a given speed
the electric field set up across the conductor by the charge the magnetic force has separated
the Hall emf, the voltage the separated charge sets up across the conductor
the current in the wire, which is the stream of moving charges the field acts on
the width of the conductor across which the Hall emf appears, or the length of wire that lies in the field
the area of the current loop, which the torque is proportional to
the number of turns in the loop or coil, each of which feels the same torque
the width of the rectangular loop, which is twice the distance from the shaft to each vertical side
the torque the field exerts on the current loop about the shaft it is mounted on
the permeability of free space, one of the basic constants of nature, exactly $4\pi \times 10^{-7}\;\text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$
the radius of the circular loop of wire whose field is wanted at its centre
the number of loops per unit length of the solenoid, $n = N/l$
the field the first wire makes at the position of the second, which is what exerts the force on it

glossary.definition: the end or the side of a magnet that is attracted toward Earth’s geographic north pole
the end or the side of a magnet that is attracted toward Earth’s geographic south pole
materials, such as iron, cobalt, nickel, and gadolinium, that exhibit strong magnetic effects
to be turned into a magnet; to be induced to be magnetic
regions within a material that behave like small bar magnets
the temperature above which a ferromagnetic material cannot be magnetized
the use of electrical currents to induce magnetism
an object that is temporarily magnetic when an electrical current is passed through it
an isolated magnetic pole; a south pole without a north pole, or vice versa (no magnetic monopole has ever been observed)
the representation of magnetic forces
another term for magnetic field
the pictorial representation of the strength and the direction of a magnetic field
the direction that the north end of a compass needle points

the rule to determine the direction of the magnetic force on a positive moving charge: when the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of the charge’s velocity $v$ and the fingers point in the direction of the magnetic field $B$, then the force on the charge is perpendicular and away from the palm; the force on a negative charge is perpendicular and into the palm
the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field
T, the SI unit of the magnetic field strength; $1\;\text{T} = \frac{1\;\text{N}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}}$
the force on a charge produced by its motion through a magnetic field; the Lorentz force
G, the unit of the magnetic field strength; $1\;\text{G} = 10^{-4}\;\text{T}$
the creation of voltage across a current-carrying conductor by a magnetic field
the electromotive force created by a current-carrying conductor by a magnetic field, $\varepsilon = Blv$

loop of wire in a magnetic field; when current is passed through the loops, the magnetic field exerts torque on the loops, which rotates a shaft; electrical energy is converted to mechanical work in the process

common application of magnetic torque on a current-carrying loop that is very similar in construction to a motor; by design, the torque is proportional to $I$ and not $\theta$, so the needle deflection is proportional to the current

a rule to determine the direction of the magnetic field induced by a current-carrying wire: Point the thumb of the right hand in the direction of current, and the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field loops

glossary.term: magnetic field strength (magnitude) produced by a long straight current-carrying wire
glossary.definition: defined as $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, where $I$ is the current, $r$ is the shortest distance to the wire, and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space
the measure of the ability of a material, in this case free space, to support a magnetic field; the constant $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\;\text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$

glossary.term: magnetic field strength at the center of a circular loop
glossary.definition: defined as $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$ where $R$ is the radius of the loop
a thin wire wound into a coil that produces a magnetic field when an electric current is passed through it

glossary.term: magnetic field strength inside a solenoid
glossary.definition: defined as $B = \mu_0 nI$ where $n$ is the number of loops per unit length of the solenoid ($n = N/l$, with $N$ being the number of loops and $l$ the length)
a physical law that describes the magnetic field generated by an electric current in terms of a specific equation

the physical law that states that the magnetic field around an electric current is proportional to the current; each segment of current produces a magnetic field like that of a long straight wire, and the total field of any shape current is the vector sum of the fields due to each segment
a set of four equations that describe electromagnetic phenomena
a medical imaging technique that uses magnetic fields create detailed images of internal tissues and organs
a phenomenon in which an externally applied magnetic field interacts with the nuclei of certain atoms
a recording of the heart’s magnetic field as it beats
a measurement of the brain’s magnetic field
